content.title: Summary of changes
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for their time and feedback. We addressed the raised questions individually for each review and made the corresponding changes in the manuscript. Below is the summary of the changes made in the updated version:
* We added the discussion on the importance of the distance parameter $\Delta_{PDE}$  for the proposed method at the end of Section 4. To support the discussion we included additional runs for parameters $\Delta_{PDE}$ and $\Delta$ in Table 3 in the appendix.
* We extended Table 3 in the appendix with studies for parameters $N$, $N_1$, $\epsilon$.
* We reproduced ‘PINN, LBFGS’ baseline runs and removed the results copied from (Krishnapriyan et al., 2021) to avoid possible confusion in Tables 1 and 4.
Minor fixes:
* We fixed the description for D set used in PL and Ens version of the proposed algorithm (line 9 in Algorithm 1).
* To improve readability, we renamed Section 3.3 to “Related work” and Section 2.2 to ‘PINNs with expansion of the time interval’.
* We removed the norm from Eq. 5.

content.title: Response to Reviewer zNYw
content.comment:
**We thank the reviewer for the detailed feedback on our paper. We appreciate the recommendations for improvements and the questions. Each question is addressed individually below.**

-          The only weakness I see is that potentially the ensemble may agree on trivial solutions. Indeed, the authors themselves write that "simple solutions can be attractive for PINNs, which can cause problems for the optimization procedure." This has been made precise theoretically in arXiv:2109.09338 and experimentally in arXiv:2203.13648, where it was shown that trivial solutions can not only be local, but actually global minima of the loss landscape. I would expect some statements how the proposed approach can escape this problem. Indeed, as can be seen in Algorithm 1, agreement of the ensemble is not sufficient for a collocation point to be considered in the training procedure: the point also has to be in close vicinity of a collocation point with confirmed accuracy (e.g., a labeled or pseudo-labeled point). This is, in my opinion, essential, and it would be interesting to see an ablation study where delta=inf.
Thank you for sharing your intuitions and the references (we were not aware of these works but our observations agree with the results reported there). It is true that all ensemble members may be attracted by the same trivial solution and the distance parameter Delta plays an important role in the success of the algorithm. We now discuss this point in the paper:

*We note the importance of hyperparameter $\Delta_\text{PDE}$ which determines how far the points considered for inclusion can be from the points already included in the loss calculations. The performance of the algorithm drops when $\Delta_\text{PDE}$ is too large. This happens because ensemble members may be attracted by the same trivial solution in areas too far away from the initial conditions, the effect caused by commonly used network architectures and initialization schemes \citep[see, e.g.,][]{wong2022learning, rohrhofer2022understanding}, which may negatively affect the ensemble diversity.*
 
**Minor Comments**:
-          In the figures, the axis labels are hardly readable.
We adjusted the axis labels in the updated version.

-          On page 5, in the enumeration at the bottom,  should probably be ? However, in both cases , because otherwise the set  does not grow in line 6 in Algorithm 1. Instead, the difference between PL and Ens is in line 9, where different sets are used for training. Please correct me if I am wrong here.
Yes, it should be L_s, we corrected it and removed clarifications on set D in brackets in the updated version. Instead, we specified in row 9 of Algorithm 1 which set is used for L_s calculation.

-          The number of iterations N is a hyperparameter for training, which would deserve to be investigated in the appendix.
We added the study of this hyperparameter in Table 3 in the appendix. 

-          In Table 1, it is interesting to see that PL, Adam has worse (but still good) results for the convection equation with beta=40. While this does not limit the merit of the proposed method, I would be interested in the underlying reasons. Could it be that the pseudo-labels are not sufficiently accurate?
Yes, this is exactly the case. PL, Adam fixes the targets for the collocation points with small variance (light blue points in Fig. 4-5) and it cannot correct inaccuracies in the target afterwards. Ens, Adam on the other hand uses the same scheduling approach as PL but allows correction of the predictions in included points throughout the training. However, if pseudo-labels are quite accurate (e.g., when two optimizers Adam and LBFGS are used) fixing them as targets helps.

content.title: Response to Reviewer wiLo
content.comment:
**We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful evaluation of our paper. We appreciate your questions and suggestions for improvements. Each individual weakness is addressed below.**

-          Weakness 1. The experiments are all single-dimensional. I'm not sure whether the proposed method works for high-dimensional x. If it works, it is better to include some high-dimensional experiments. If it doesn't work, why?
We haven’t tried high-dimensional equations in our experiments. We considered equations commonly used in the PINN literature.

-          Weakness 2. A new training point is added to the training set only if the variance of prediction is smaller than some pre-defined threshold (Line 14 in Algorithm 1). I wonder is there any case that no data points satisfy the criteria? If so, is there any possibility that the algorithm will stuck when sigma are too small? If not, is there any theoretical guarantee? Thanks!
Yes, it can happen. The ablation for the values of sigma in Table 3 shows that the convergence speed slows down for smaller sigmas and there are seeds where not all the points are included by the time when the update budget is used.

content.title: Response to Reviewer PC3y
content.comment:
**We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful feedback on our paper. We address the concerns below.**

-          The method is based on the time adaptation/marching idea, and the novelty is small.
Our proposed adaptation scheme is more flexible and allows us to extend the domain in both directions (time and space) which were not possible in previous works. This flexibility makes it possible to propagate the solution from several locations, as we illustrate in Figure 1.

-          Compared to other methods, even the very standard PINN, the improvement is small. In most cases, the proposed method is still worse than other methods.
Even though the proposed method doesn’t lead to the best result on all of the tested equations, it works consistently well for all of the considered systems. 

-          The proposed method trains an ensemble of 5 PINNs, and thus has 5x higher computational cost. To make a fair comparison, other baselines should use 5x more training points.
It is correct that our method has a higher computational cost compared to the baselines. In our implementation, the forward and backward computations of an ensemble of five PINNs on the average takes 27% more time compared to a single PINN (due to parallelization of computations). We do not agree that providing 5x more points to other baselines would be a fair comparison. Providing the same computational budget for all comparison methods might be more fair, but this would require a major investment in code optimization of all the baselines. We have made the decision to fix the number of training points and the number of parameter updates.

-          All the examples tested in the paper are still simple, and more challenging examples are needed.
We tested on equations commonly considered in other papers in this field. 

-          The idea of adding new points based on the current PINN solution is highly related to adaptive sampling methods for training points. Comparison with these methods are also needed.
Adaptive sampling techniques have the benefits of increasing the size of the “training set” (collocation points) during training. Such techniques may in principle be combined with other ideas from the PINN literature including the ideas proposed in our paper. For that reason, we opted for not including these methods but rather fixing the size of the “training set” (the number of collocation points) for all the comparison methods.

content.title: Response to Reviewer esVi (part 2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the detailed and thorough review of our paper and the recommendations for improvement. We address the questions and concerns below.

**Please find below the answers to individual questions (part 2).**

-          Q: -- As far as I understood, some of the results are directly taken from Krishnapriyan et al., 2021 without reproducing them. It is unclear whether exactly the same data sets and seeds were used for obtaining the results in Krishnapriyan et al., 2021 (I suppose not). Thus it appears that these results cannot be simply copy-pasted into the table.
We are quite sure that the numbers copied from (Krishnapriyan et al., 2021) are comparable with the other numbers: We carefully followed the evaluation protocol of that paper and the ballpark of our results obtained with PINN, LBFGS was similar to the numbers reported in (Krishnapriyan et al., 2021). However, to address this concern, we decided to remove the results from (Krishnapriyan et al., 2021) from the revised version of the paper, replacing them with our own results obtained for PINN, LBFGS.

-          Q: -- Not that much attention is given to hyperparameter ϵ (only referenced from the original paper, but no hyperparameter results in table 3 or 4).
We added the ablation for values of hyperparameter $\epsilon$ to Table 3 in the Appendix: This hyperparameter does not influence the results much.

-          Q: -- In table A3 the default number of networks is not considered for some reason.
The results for values of hyperparameters used in the main paper are included in the row named ‘default’. The number of networks L=5 corresponds to ‘default’.

-          Q: -- In table A3 it seems that in some cases 3/10 networks did not converge, yet the results appear to be fairly good, which is surprising. Perhaps it is worth elaborating on why non-convergent cases still lead to fairly good results.
We have added the following explanation to the first paragraph of Appendix A.3:
*In Table 3, we test the sensitivity of the ensemble training of PINNs to its hyperparameters. In these experiments, we use the number of updates as described in Appendix A.2. We consider that a run has not converged if less than 95% of the sampled points have been added to the set which is used to compute L_pde by the last update. Such runs are excluded from the statistics reported in Table 3.*
This means that runs marked as non-converged in Table 3 may contain accurate solutions (at least in the points included in the calculation by the time we stop the run) but they need more iterations to include all pre-sampled collocation points.

**Reproducibility comments**:
-          The proposed method itself is clear and well-described; however, the paper lacks an extensive explanation of the results. There are some mistakes and unclarities, which are described in the detailed comments. The code was not included for reproducibility. Some of the results included in the comparison tables from other studies are simply copy-pasted, which might result in biased if those were run on different data sets with different seeds.

The code for our method was included as a zip folder attached to the submission as under supplementary materials. After the submission is de-anonymized, a link to a GitHub repo will be provided. In the updated version, we removed results reported in prior work.

content.title: Response to Reviewer esVi (part 1)
content.comment:
**We thank the reviewer for the detailed and thorough review of our paper and the recommendations for improvement. We address the questions and concerns below.**

-          Q: -- Is there a term missing in eq. 6 for the loss of the boundary condition? Should there not be a term -b_i similarly to -u_i in eq. 5?
Without the loss of generality, we formulate the boundary conditions in Eq. 3 such that the right-hand side of the equation is always equal to zero. For example, for the boundary conditions of the Dirichlet type
u(X_1,t) = u*(t),
functional g is (u(X_1,t) - u*(t)).

-          Q: -- Unclear why in eq. 7, there is no L2 norm anymore (compared to eq. 5 and 6); is there a reason it is not used in the loss for PDE?
We removed the norm from (5).

-          Q: -- The last paragraph of 2.2 (related work) states: “The method can be combined with the time adaptive sampling strategies and very recently the method has been combined with an evolutionary sampling strategy (Daw et al., 2022).” – it’s unclear how this is relevant to this paper or in what way it is an advantage of causality training approach. More clarification on what role the time adaptive sampling or evolutionary sampling play here would be nice.
We removed the sentence from this paragraph to avoid the confusion and left out the discussion on sampling methods to the appendix since sampling methods can be combined both with the baseline and our method. 

-          Q: -- Overall, paragraph 2.2. can be strengthened; the link between related work and the proposed approach is not explicit enough.
More explicit comparison between the closest baselines and our method is available in section 3.3. 
To improve readability, we renamed section 3.3 to “Related work” and section 2.2 to ‘PINNs with expansion of the time interval’ in the updated version.

-          Q:  -- Section 3: motivation relies on the model introduced in section 4. This is a personal preference, but I would suggest either explaining the motivation without referring to the equations of the next section or already introducing them here.
We removed the reference to the equations from this section in the updated version.  

-          Q: -- Background on the considered differential equations discussed in eq.9-17 would be beneficial for a wider audience;
In the refined version we added clarifications on where the equations are used. 
  
**Comments on the results**:
-          Q: -- Only 5 networks in ensembles were considered, which is quite a low number; why did the authors not consider more networks in the ensembles? In the Appendix, the robustness check considers up to 7 networks. Do you expect the results to improve with a further increase in the number of networks?
We try to keep the number of the networks in the ensemble small (to reduce the computational overhead) but sufficient to provide enough information to determine a schedule for point inclusion. In the ablation studies (see Table 3), we show that using L=10 networks in the ensemble does not change the results significantly.   

-          Q: -- Only 10 seeds are considered in Table 1, which is very little to make general conclusions, at least 100 runs should be included in these results.
We agree that increasing the number of random seeds would provide more information. Unfortunately, due to limited computational resources we had to cut the number of seeds to 10. Note that in prior works on PINNs, the results are often reported on 1 to 5 runs without reporting the standard deviation.  

-          Q: -- In Table 2, in some cases, vanilla PIN with Adam + LBFGS outperforms ensembles of PINNs. Do the authors have an intuition of why this happens?
We hypothesize that because of the shape of the correct solution for these problems, the Adam optimizer finds a good starting point for the LBFGS-finetuning, which results in the good performance of PINN, Adam+LBFGS.

-          Q: -- In some results for ensembles (Table 2), standard deviations for ensembles are large. Would not we generally expect a lower standard deviation for ensemble methods? If so, does this mean that only having 5 networks is perhaps not sufficient?
The number of ensemble members primarily affects the schedule in which the collocation points are included into the loss computations, not the variance of the obtained results (note that the results in Table 2 are averages across random seeds, not ensemble members). Therefore, we generally cannot expect that the variance (across seeds) would decrease as the number of ensemble members grows.

-          Q: -- In Table 1 it appears that some wrong results are highlighted as the best, in particular for the reaction-diffusion experiment.
We selected the best results with standard deviation in mind. For example, we highlight ‘bc-PINN, Adam+LBFGS’ value 6.51 +/- 0.13 instead of ‘SA-PINN’ with 5.94 +/- 1.63 for reaction-diffusion equation with $\nu=4$ due to high std of SA-PINN.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to use ensembles for PINNs to deal with the difficulties of training. In particular, one problem that arises when training PINNs is that they can converge to a wrong solution. The approach is motivated by the fact that individual PINNs provide a similar solution at the points where observations (i.e. observed data or initial conditions) are available, but the solutions can be significantly different further away from these points, and thus using ensembles can improve the stability of training.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:

Strengths: 
-- The method appears to have the potential to improve the stability of training PINNs;
-- The method is easy to implement;

Weaknesses:
-- Weak evaluations and unclear choices in some experimental set-ups (as such, it is hard to conclude whether the method indeed improves the stability);
-- Minor mistakes and unclarities persist throughout the paper;
-- Failure modes of the proposed method remain somewhat unclear, and overall intuition or explanation of the results is missing;

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a novel method to adaptively sample training data for PINN. The authors noticed that the PDE loss is meaningless for samples with large t. The proposed solution is to use samples with small t at first, then gradually add samples according to the variance of ensemble predictions. It is shown that the proposed method can lead to good results for several different PDEs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: the authors made a good observation and figured out the internal reason for the hardiness of training of PINN. The proposed solution is a nature solution once the reason was figured out. The "red dots", "blue dots" and "black dots" figures are a very clear visualization of the main idea which makes the paper reader-friendly.

Weakness: 1. The experiments are all single-dimensional. I'm not sure whether the proposed method works for high-dimensional x. If it works, it is better to include some high-dimensional experiments. If it doesn't work, why?
2. A new training point is added to the training set only if the variance of prediction is smaller than some pre-defined threshold (Line 14 in Algorithm 1). I wonder is there any case that no data points satisfy the criteria? If so, is there any possibility that the algorithm will stuck when sigma are too small? If not, is there any theoretical guarantee? Thanks!
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is written clearly with high quality, especially the figures are very helpful to readers. The novelty seems good. I didn't reproduce the work.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposed a novel method to adaptively draw training samples during the training of PINN. Variance of predictions are used as criteria for adding new samples. Experiments show that the proposed algorithm outperforms other methods, but are limited to single-dimensional cases.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes ensembles of PINNs to improve training stability. Specifically, the authors propose to use only those collocation points for evaluating the PDE residual that are close to regions in the computational domain for which the ensemble has achieved sufficient agreement. The proposed method performs well on several systems of PDEs and outperforms other approaches that sample or weight collocation points adaptively.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is very well written. The proposed method is simple to understand, intuitively appealing, and yet effective. The experimental evidence is convincing. In summary, the paper is an excellent contribution to improving PINN training.

The only weakness I see is that potentially the ensemble may agree on trivial solutions. Indeed, the authors themselves write that "simple solutions can be attractive for PINNs, which can cause problems for the optimization procedure." This has been made precise theoretically in arXiv:2109.09338 and experimentally in arXiv:2203.13648, where it was shown that trivial solutions can not only be local, but actually global minima of the loss landscape.

I would expect some statements how the proposed approach can escape this problem. Indeed, as can be seen in Algorithm 1, agreement of the ensemble is not sufficient for a collocation point to be considered in the training procedure: the point also has to be in close vicinity of a collocation point with confirmed accuracy (e.g., a labeled or pseudo-labeled point). This is, in my opinion, essential, and it would be interesting to see an ablation study where $\Delta=\infty$.

### Minor Comments:
- In the figures, the axis labels are hardly readable.
- On page 5, in the enumeration at the bottom, $\mathcal{L}$ should probably be $\mathcal{L}s$? However, in both cases $D=D_L \cup D_{PL}$, because otherwise the set $D$ does not grow in line 6 in Algorithm 1. Instead, the difference between PL and Ens is in line 9, where different sets are used for training. Please correct me if I am wrong here.
- The number of iterations $N$ is a hyperparameter for training, which would deserve to be investigated in the appendix.
- In Table 1, it is interesting to see that PL, Adam has worse (but still good) results for the convection equation with $\beta=40$. While this does not limit the merit of the proposed method, I would be interested in the underlying reasons. Could it be that the pseudo-labels are not sufficiently accurate?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written and of high quality. The approach is valid and the results are excellent. The novelty is limited, since several other adaptive sampling schemes have already been proposed. This does not limit the merit of the paper, however, since previous comparable approaches seem to be outperformed.
content.summary_of_the_review: An excellent paper about a timely topic. Its limited novelty is outweighed by the intuitive approach and the convincing experimental evidence.

content.title: Improved Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Model Ensembles
content.abstract: Learning the solution of partial differential equations (PDEs) with a neural network is an attractive alternative to traditional solvers due to its elegance, greater flexibility and the ease of incorporating observed data. However, training such physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) is notoriously difficult in practice since PINNs often converge to wrong solutions. In this paper, we propose a training algorithm that starts approximation of the PDE solution in the neighborhood of initial conditions and gradually expands the solution domain based on agreement of an ensemble of PINNs. PINNs in the ensemble find similar solutions in the vicinity of points with targets (e.g., observed data or initial conditions) while the found solutions may substantially differ farther away from the observations. Therefore, we propose to use the ensemble agreement as the criterion for gradual expansion of the solution interval, that is including new points for computing the loss derived from differential equations. Due to the flexibility of the domain expansion, our algorithm can easily incorporate measurements in arbitrary locations. In contrast to the existing PINN algorithms with time-adaptive strategies, the proposed algorithm does not need a pre-defined schedule of interval expansion and it treats time and space equally. We experimentally show that the proposed algorithm can stabilize PINN training and yield performance competitive to the recent variants of PINNs trained with time adaptation.
